points.text: Your feeds table is partitioned by region, but a feed belongs to one user. Rows for all users in a region pile into the same partition, and there is no per-user key to fetch exactly one user's feed even though the index helps. Partition by user_id instead.
points.quote: table kv.feeds(region pk, user_id, posts, updated_at) index(user_id)

Your write only records the post itself plus an invalidation. No queue, worker or fanout updates the followers' feed rows, so GET_FEED cannot return the newest 20 posts from people they follow — new posts never reach any feed. Hand writes to a worker that merges the post into each follower's feed.

A counter-based generator gives codes in counting order, so anyone can enumerate zt.to/a1, a2, a3 and open links meant for other recipients. For promo SMS sent to individuals, think about whether guessable codes matter; a non-sequential scheme avoids that while still guaranteeing uniqueness.

In this sql table user_id is the primary key, so only one row may exist per user. A user in more than one match or offer batch silently overwrites the earlier pending job, losing a send the statement says must never be lost. You need a unique job id as the key and the user as an indexed column.

In a sql table the primary key must be unique per row, so using game_id alone collapses all players of a game into one row that overwrites itself on every submit. Make the key unique per player within a game, for example game_id plus player_id, so top-100 and per-player scores survive.

Your counter row is keyed only by user, so it must live forever and never resets — after a hundred total calls the user is blocked permanently, but the limit is per minute. The key needs to encode the minute window so old counters expire naturally.

You store a rank column per player, but SUBMIT_SCORE only sends player_id, game_id and score, so every submit would have to recompute the ranks of the whole game, which is racy under concurrent submits. Better to keep rank derived: select the top rows ordered by score, not store the position.

A player's score should probably be replaced, not appended: players keep posting new scores each question. Think about whether SUBMIT_SCORE upserts by player and game or keeps a history for every answer, since that changes what the top-100 query must skip over.

You check that a seat is free and then write it taken, but the nosql store has no compare-and-set across partitions, so two fans booking the same seat between check and write both succeed. The strict no-double-sale rule cannot be kept this way.

points.text: The core need is a transactional or atomic conditional write per seat. A partitioned key-value store does not offer that, which is what makes the double-sale race possible; think about whether the store type fits this guarantee.

The table stores only chat_id, message_id and body, so GET_MESSAGES cannot order the chat or pick its recent messages. A random message id does not carry time, so a read cannot sort messages by when they were sent. The table also lacks a sender, which a chat read would want.

Your message ids are random, so they give no ordering across nodes even if they never repeat. A chat application usually wants ids ordered by time so the store itself can order messages; a snowflake-style id generation would carry the sending order.

BOOK must return a booking id, but the request replies the moment it enters the queue; the ids and db steps run in the worker after the client is gone. The caller cannot get the booking id, and the response can claim success before the seat is actually taken.
points.quote: write BOOK:      client > lb > api ~> queue > worker > ids > db then invalidate cache

points.text: Your read-your-writes promise depends on the cache only for miss-through reads plus invalidation, but the queue in the write path means the booking may not be committed when the caller refetches the seat map, so stale-free views are not guaranteed.

The worker delivers the push first and records it afterwards. If the worker dies in between, the user may get the notification even though no row is written, or a retry after a crash delivers it twice. Recording the accepted send at accept time and updating status as you deliver makes retries safe.

In the seats table the primary key is show_id, so there can be only one row per show: booking one seat overwrites the last row sold and you cannot track every seat's status. The key must let many rows coexist per show, one per seat, so each seat's status is its own row.

The write goes straight to a feeds row and ends: nothing fans the post out to the followers' feeds. Readers who follow the poster get a feed that never includes the new post, so GET_FEED can return a feed missing an accepted post.
points.quote: write POST:     client > lb > api > ids > kv then invalidate cache

points.text: Fan-out done synchronously in the POST route couples publishing to the feed stores; if delivering to feeds fails after the accept, the post exists but feeds are incomplete. Handing feed updates to the queue with workers would decouple the accept from fan-out.
